text: Good afternoon and welcome to the February 27th meeting of the Legislative Committee. As our busiest time of the year gets underway with the county executive presenting his proposal of the FY 2027 budget last week, the 2026 legislative session is quickly ending, with adjournment now less than two weeks away.

We did not hold the Legislative Committee last week, as many of us were in Richmond for the annual reception with our Fairfax County General Assembly delegation. It was a great opportunity to continue connecting, collaborating, and discussing our priorities. Last Sunday, both the House and Senate chambers presented their budget proposals.

As such, our format will look a little bit different this week. After an update of our county initiatives, we will move directly into a high-level overview of both chambers' budget proposals and allow time for questions immediately following each presentation.

There are no bills set for discussion today. We will instead immediately move to recommended bills and, finally, legislative updates. Before I pass it over to Jennifer, I want to highlight the progress on legislation related to our housing bills and our housing bills for local employees.

HB 164, co-patroned by many of our Fairfax County representatives, eliminates current restrictions on home ownership grants that localities may provide to their employers. This gives local governments a practical tool to help our workforce afford to live in the communities they serve and support long-term workforce retention.

On one additional note, and with perfect timing during National Evasive Species Awareness Week, Senator Saddam Salim's bill on evasive species passed the House and is awaiting vote in the Senate. This legislation aligns closely with Fairfax County's Evasive Species Ordinance that we adopted two years ago.

With that being said, Jennifer, I will now pass it on to you. Jennifer Vaney, legislative director. Thank you, chairman. Welcome to two weeks before. So last Sunday was budget Sunday, but let's first give you an update on our three initiatives. The urban public private partnership fund is still in the exact same phase. It has been the last several times we talked. The Senate passed a study version. It will come before house rules. I have talked with that chairman. I am, I'm, I'm optimistic, but that is something where a lot of bills die. So we're hopeful a study at least gets through to use a tool for the future,

but that's where that one stands, and I'll turn it over to Lori to talk about the Park Authority. Lori Sims. I just wanted to let everybody know that HB 250 that Watts carried on our behalf has passed the Senate unanimously. So just as a recap for everybody, it passed the House and it passed the Senate. So we're excited to hear about the legislation carrying all the way through.

Good afternoon, Christine Prentiss, Government Relations Associate for Fairfax County DOT. Last night in Senate Transportation, HB 55, our muffler bill, passed out of committee 7 to 6 with two abstentions.

It will be on the floor early next week of the Senate, and we will be pushing hard to get it through there. Thank you. All right. We'll roll right into the budget. I'm going to invite our DMB support up to the table.

I just wanted to start off the discussion to give you a little bit of the lay of the land. So a lot of years when the House and the Senate will have different budgets and different priorities, this year they are actually very fundamentally different. And so we're going to go through some of the details, but it's very unclear at this point what of each budget we'll go into too, because not only are the budgets different in how they're choosing to spend money, the Senate put a tax proposal in to sunset the data center sales tax exemption, which gives them an additional

$1.2 billion to spend. And so that just means that these budgets are fundamentally different. But then on top of that, again, they also are choosing to spend on different priorities. So we'll go over the budget, but I wanted to set a little bit of a leveling of there isn't a lot of confidence, or we don't feel like these budgets necessarily give us a clear direction of how, what will happen when this goes to conference. So I'm going to turn it, so the very first portion of, there's a, the Fairfax County House and Senate Budget Overview Sheet.

The first section is tax proposals, so you'll see at the top, the House decided to handle that a tax, a data center tax exemption, tying it to meeting certain environmental standards to qualify for it, the Senate gets rid of it altogether. The Senate had a couple other provisions in there, such as increasing standard deductions and extending that sunset, as well as another tax re-rate program. And you'll see how that plays out specifically related to transit funding. So I'll go ahead and turn it over to Elbena at this point.

Mr. Chairman, members of the committee, Albano Senovo from the budget office. So on K-12 funding, I just wanted to note that the handout that's posted online and that you have with you doesn't have the Senate impacts to FCPS because we were still working through the analysis.

But since then, I've heard from them, and we work closely with the school budget staff. So I'll be speaking to the impacts of the Senate amendments as well. So on compensation, the House included an amendment in the caboose impacting fiscal year 26.

They included additional funding for a one-time bonus of $1,500 for instructional and support positions. These bonuses may be provided in fiscal year 26 or 27. And this bonus is instead of the proposed 2% bonus that was included in the introduced budget, FCPS is estimated to receive $10.7 million towards the cost of this bonus from the state.

However, the total cost to them would be $48 million. So after accounting for the state share, the net cost to FCPS would still be $37.6 million. And then in the Senate budget, the Senate included additional funding to provide a 3% compensation increase to teachers.
This compares to the 2% that was included in the introduced budget. So FCPS would receive $6.6 million in fiscal year '27 over the introduced budget for the 3% salary increase.

And then the House includes a one-time flexibility payment. They included $400 million in fiscal year '27 for a one-time flexible payment for school divisions, and this could be used throughout the biennium, either in '27 or '28, but again, it is a one-time funding.

To access these funds, the school divisions must certify that they have provided 2% compensatory increases in each fiscal year. And FCPS is estimated to receive $37.9 million in one-time funding in fiscal year '27 as a result of this amendment.

And then both the House and the Senate budgets include additional funding for special education add-on, which was a recommendation from the JLARC study. The House includes a lot more-- $74 million in each fiscal year to increase the add-on rates applied to basic aid for special education students.

And FCPS would receive $10.5 million in fiscal year '27. In the Senate, there's $12.8 million in each year. It increases the add-on percentage slightly. And FCPS would receive $1.4 million in fiscal year '27.

And then the Senate also includes additional funding to increase the at-risk add-on, $49 million in both years, general funding, and then additional revenue of $20 million in '28 as a result of the skill games revenues.

From that, FCPS would receive $1.4 million in '27. The Senate budget also includes additional funding of $60 million as a result of the skill games to provide an increase to the infrastructure and operations per pupil amount.

This is only in fiscal year '28. And FCPS would receive $5.5 million in '28. There's also, as Jennifer mentioned, the Senate proposes to eliminate the sales tax exemption for data centers effective January 1, 2027.

As a result of that, there's additional sales tax revenue that would also go to public education funding. So the Senate budget recognizes this, includes additional funding, and FCPS is estimated to receive $9.3 million in FY27 as a result of this.

The Senate also included additional funding to support school breakfast to increase the reimbursement amount, and FCPS would receive $700,000 in FY27. However, this doesn't go to their operating fund.
It goes to their school nutrition fund. And lastly, on the school's items, there's a policy change that is proposed in the calculation of the local composite index for the next biennium.

It proposes to add to the computation the value of computer equipment and peripherals used in data centers. And we don't know what the impact to FCPS's LCI would be, but obviously in Northern Virginia we have a lot more of the data center equipment, so it would likely be negative for Northern Virginia as a whole.

And so to summarize, for fiscal year 27, the House budget compared to the introduced budget, FCPS would receive an additional $10.5 million in recurring funds, and as I mentioned, $37.9 million in one-time funds.

So the total is $48.4 million in operating funds. And then in the Senate version of the budget, compared to the governor's introduced budget, FCPS would receive an additional $18.6 million in operating funds and $700,000 for their school nutrition fund.

And I would stop here to see if there's any questions on those school items, or I can continue. page two under compensation and the compensation board just wanted to know that the county's initiative to restore unfunded positions in local directors of finance offices was not included in the House or the Senate budget also not included is additional funding for HB 599 for aid to localities with police

departments. The introduced budget had included level funding with fiscal year 26, so there's no increase there. And as a reminder, the House includes the same raises for state employees, teachers, and state-supported local employees as the introduced budget at 2%. And then the Senate raises to 3%. The salary increases for state employees and teachers, but leaves the state supported local employees at 2%.

And I wanted to note, there's a House amendment that would direct the Compensation Board to factor into their next workload evaluation for commissioners of revenue and finance directors the work that is required to review applications for tax exemptions for 100% disabled veterans.

And actually, we have noted on page 6, Under the other items of interest, a similar amendment that would actually establish a joint subcommittee of the General Assembly to analyze the rising cost of those mandatory property exemptions for disabled veterans and their families.

And we noted that for tax year 25, Fairfax County provided $63 million in real estate tax relief for disabled veterans and surviving spouses as a result of this state mandate. And actually since 2011, the cost of this program to the county has been $287 million.

And we've seen rapid growth in the number of applications and the amounts that we've been relieving. And since 2020, there has been an average annual increase of almost 30% per year. So then going back to page three, just to go over some of the housing items, there's almost a full list of amendments in both the House and the Senate.

I'll just mention the House provides $25 million in fiscal year 27 to capitalize the Virginia Housing Revolving Loan Fund that was established by HB 820. And also the House provides an additional $12.5 million in fiscal year 27 to deposit into the Virginia Housing Trust Fund, which our legislative program supports additional funding to this housing trust fund. And actually

the Senate includes more, an additional $50 million for the Virginia Housing Trust Fund. However, a portion of it, $20.6 million, is earmarked for a pilot program for mixed income housing development. And then there's a couple of smaller items. However, I just wanted to point out, in the House, there's $363,000 each year for HB 804, which was related to the statewide housing targets. And this is a legislation that the county opposes unless it's amended
to address our concerns around the limiting local flexibility. And then there's an additional funding, $161,000 each year for HB 374. That was related to Manufactured Home Lot Rental Act.
HB 374 is legislation that the county supports. And then in the Senate version, there's additional $261,000 each year to make available data on new and existing housing developments in each area.

And this is legislation. It's SB 666 and the county seeking to amend to address our concerns around overly burdensome reporting requirements. Well, thank you so much. I think in between these sections here and before we jump into health and human services and transportation might be good just to take a quick pause.

Mr. Chairman, do you have any comments or questions? I'm good. I want to ask our board. Supervisor Raschner Heiser. Thank you. Just a quick question on the school funding. Just a little confusion I have. That's what I'm trying to get at. So my understanding is that it's not in addition to what they're already giving. They would qualify for this funding. That's what I was trying to clarify to make sure it wasn't a separate increase that the state was required. No, they didn't note additional expenditures to them to be able to.

That's what I was trying to clarify. Thank you. Supervisor Bierman. So Christina might know the answer to this. I believe that their budget already assumed that they were getting some extra money due to the 2% compensation increase, but this says that there would be additional money if they went up to a 3% compensation increase, and I believe that their budget already predicted more than a 3% increase, so it would, so in other words, their budget assumed 2%, so the 2% they already factored in from the state, going to 3%, this would be an additional,

this would be additional money as long as they go above 3%. Additional over what they already thought they were getting and factored in, correct? Yeah. So, you know, Albena mentioned that, sorry, Christina Jackson, CFO, that under the Senate amendments, they would get another 6.6, which would be the state share of that additional 1% going from 2 to 3.

So going into human services, not on the sheet, but just wanted to verbally call out that both Medicaid and SNAP and the implementation requirements around H.R.1 did receive some funding in the budget for new tech or work to try to get the error rates down, so that is included in the budget.

And again, when we give you a more full update, a full analysis next week, those will all be listed in there, but I know that's a big priority and a big concern. And the state is covering the cost for the administration fee, which is the one that we had concerns about. So I wanted to highlight those.

Again, that will be in the full packet we give you. On page four, it talks about the CSA, the Children's Services Act CAP. We discussed this when we talked about budget amendments, and so basically this is the state, again, they did not remove the 2.5% cap.

So you might remember last year they had a 5% cap for all private day placements. Now they've lowered that even further to 2.5%. Private day is considered a mandatory service, which means it has to be paid for, which means any gap between them will have to come from us versus a shared responsibility with the state.

So we have concerns about that. They did include some language requested by VACO that is around studying why private day placements continue to go up, as that is a huge driver of the cost increase for CSA across.

And so we're hopeful that that could present future solutions instead of them continuing to cap their portion of it. And then one budget did put in $10 million for the CISNA, and I'm going to fail at what that stands for, but it's special funding from the federal level for the very specific and high needs, special needs in the school system.

So the House includes additional money and a request to broaden the characteristics of what that covers, which they think will help address some of these private day. The Senate asked the Department of Education to study how we could go about doing that and doing CISNA better.

So that's the CSA. The other thing I wanted to quick highlight is right below it as the child welfare reform we've talked about. We'll talk about the updates to the bills, but you'll see here the House still assumes that they're moving forward on the centralization of intake, but just staggered, so they kept a lot of the money in.

The Senate assumed that they are waiting two years so that they took that $30 million in that was put there and redirected it to other priorities. The other thing I wanted to highlight was on page five, middle of the page, under natural, the last bullet under natural and historic resources.

I did want to just draw attention to there was additional language requiring Virginia and agencies to get back into RGGI. No, that's been a priority, so I wanted to call out to that before I turn it over for questions or to Noel. Well, thank you so much, Jennifer. And just real quick before I pass it over, see if Chairman McKay would like to comment on any of this.

And the whole country saw that we were stepping away from that. We need to be leading. We don't need to be stepping backwards. And so I think that with our new governor is an opportunity to get back into Reggie, get back into leading on environmental issues throughout the Commonwealth. Obviously, and this morning I actually published an op-ed in the Richmond Times with House Majority Leader Sean O'Harring on the importance of getting back into Reggie.

So I'm really excited, glad to hear the good news, and looking forward to the signing from the governor on this. Mr. Chairman, do you have any comments or questions? Yeah, I just want to go back to page four for a minute under the child welfare reform. I'm looking at the bottom of page four, and I'm looking at what's in red.

And I know we talked about this before. I know the county generally does not support moving to a centralized CPS intake system. I guess the question is, does it look like there's broad support in the state to move to that?

because I still think that's in the interest of everywhere in Virginia except us. And I don't want to look cold-hearted here to the realities that there's room for a lot of improvement in other parts of the state, and I don't want to appear like we don't care about that because we do.

We just want to protect our interests. So can you give me an update on where it's tracking legislatively and what the likelihood of it being approved is? Yeah, and if you want to look at where the bills are in the packet, I can also call out the numbers of that as we do that update. If you want to just tell us verbally on that, it's fine.

Okay, so basically the bills right now are doing the fund dance of the Senate's conforming to the House and the House is conforming to the Senate. The basic differences are the House version assumes that we're moving forward with centralization no matter what, but they do do a work group and a study about how do we do this well, how do we do this better.

The Senate delays everything two years, puts in very specific language about needing a neutral third party to do a study and then doing a work group to see if this is actually the solution, because I think there's a lot of concerns that the McKinsey report that came out that had a lot of this data, it kind of assumed that this was the only solution, that there was a problem and this was a solution, but it wasn't necessarily one for one, which is what our concerns were.

And so the Senate approach, which is our more favorable, the one we favor more, is actually stepping back and taking a look of like, would this actually solve the problem or are there other problems we need to solve. And one of the considerations they've talked about is, could we do either phased in or do we do regions? Or is it a, you can do your own, but you could also have the ability to do a state. So kind of a hybrid approach of some people like Fairfax being able to keep their own system that they're really proud of and they do a lot of really great work in. While other systems that would actually like the state support in taking

this over would have that option too. I mean, to me, it sounds like, like you said, the Senate version is a lot better. I just, I know this is for us. I just want to be, I still think we need to be careful about the declarative. We do not support moving to it because to your point, we don't have all the data and information and frankly, it should be studied and there should be an analysis done and there should be opportunities for jurisdictions that do this well to continue to do what we're doing while they can still make improvements in other parts of the So I just want to point out that nuance because I think it's if we're asked for our position It shouldn't just be we're opposed to this. It should be we think doing the study makes sense
